rv.q: The new regime at the National Theatre has delivered its first bona fide hit in Robert Hastie's five-star revival
A pure pleasure in terms of the acting and the staging.
It's a glorious final swell of a vast production, which sets the sun on these summerfolk.

With more than 20 characters and a substantial running time, it needs hefty resources; and it needs its moment. Trevor Nunn staged it in the National’s Olivier Theatre, on the eve of the millennium, with a crack cast.

The satire is less subtle than Chekhov’s and made more humorous in Robert Hastie’s period-dress production of this new adaptation by sibling playwrights Nina and Moses Raine. Their version has a comic lilt, with added swearing and raunch – but is faithful to the original, sometimes to the letter.

Though the sprawling production’s energy flags at times and we never spend quite long enough on any one character, this remains a melancholy, impressionistic portrait of an era – like our own – marked by vacuousness and poised on the brink of sudden upheaval.
So this is a generational production, really, and whatever its flaws are, they shouldn’t put you off seeing the sort of luxury revival that the NT was made for.

There’s a woodland world, giving way to a stream in which the actors dip their toes. The play’s strength lies in the superb roles for women. I for one completely fell for Sophie Rundle (star of Gentleman Jack) as Varvara, wife of an oafish lawyer (Paul Ready - terrific).
This version of Summerfolk, directed with verve by Robert Hastie, is 40 minutes shorter than its last incarnation on the National’s stage, when Trevor Nunn directed it some 25 years ago.
Guilty of the excesses it seeks to satirise, the production certainly won’t discomfort today’s middle classes.

In many ways, it feels like a play ripe for revival, speaking clearly to the present moment. At its centre lies a pressing question: does anything really matter when the world is falling apart? Yet, despite the hazy glow of this new version by siblings Nina Raine and Moses Raine, it’s a message that lands with a heavy hand.
Still, the best moments of Summerfolk shine out, strikingly modern.

That manifest wisdom gives her vicious denunciation of an entire class of intelligentsia at a nightmarish end of summer dinner party all the more force, director Robert Hastie’s slow build to that climax fully vindicated.

And now here they are, back at the venerable venue in Maxim Gorky’s 1905 full-frontal attack on the demographic. His play is a response to Chekhov’s much more sympathetic The Cherry Orchard, which was written just two years earlier.
Whilst it is widely lauded as a frenetic ensemble piece, there are key characters who will always need to make an impression if the whole is to have been deemed successful.
So as the characters ponder the purpose of their lives, the audience is left to wonder about the purpose of the play.
